steps.body: An equation is a balanced scale: 2x + 3 = 11 says the two pans weigh the same. You can take tiles away — but only if you take the SAME amount off BOTH pans. Take from one side only and the beam tips: the two sides stop being equal, and the equation you're holding is no longer the one you started with.
Solve your first equation by moving the tiles themselves.

predict.prompt: If you take 3 unit tiles off ONLY the left pan of 2x + 3 = 11, what happens to the beam?

options.label: It stays level — the x-tiles keep it steady
It tips — the right pan is now heavier
It tips the other way — the left pan gets heavier

predict.reveal: The beam tips toward the right pan. Taking 3 off the left made that side lighter, and nothing changed on the right — so the sides are no longer equal. Every fair move comes in pairs: what leaves the left must leave the right.

widget.prompt: Solve 2x + 3 = 11. Clear the unit tiles from both pans, then split both sides into equal groups.
widget.successFeedback: x = 4. Three units left each pan (2x = 8), then both sides split into 2 groups — one x-tile against 4 units.
widget.unbalancedFeedback: The beam tipped — tiles left one pan only. Undo, and this time pair every removal: one off the left, one off the right.
widget.notIsolatedFeedback: Balanced the whole way — every move was fair. But x isn't alone yet. Clear the remaining units from both sides, then use the split button.
widget.missFeedback: The x-tiles are the thing you're solving for — keep them on the pan. Clear the UNIT tiles from both sides, then split both sides into equal groups.

cml.actionGoal: Apply legal inverse operations to both sides and preserve the solution set at every move.
cml.counterfactualPrompt: Apply an operation to only one side on purpose. What breaks, and how would you repair the trace?

explanation.prompt: Why must the same legal operation be applied to both sides?

options.label: It creates an equivalent equation with the same solutions.
options.feedback: Exactly. Balanced transformations preserve equality and the solution set.

options.label: The two sides can be changed independently as long as x is isolated.
options.feedback: That describes a surface feature, not the mathematical relationship that must remain true. Balanced transformations preserve equality and the solution set.

explanationVariants: Take 3 units off each pan to get 4x = 12, then split both sides into 4 equal groups: x = 3.
Units first, groups second: clearing the + 3 leaves the x-tiles alone on the left, and only then can the pans be shared out evenly.

widget.successFeedback: x = 3. The pans stayed level through every move: 4x + 3 = 15, then 4x = 12, then x = 3.
widget.unbalancedFeedback: The beam tipped, so somewhere a tile came off one side without its partner leaving the other. Undo back to level, then remove in pairs.
widget.notIsolatedFeedback: Still level — good. Now finish: get every unit tile off the left pan (matching each removal on the right), then split.
widget.missFeedback: Don't remove the x-tiles — x is what the question asks for. Clear units from both sides, then split both sides into 4 groups.

steps.body: Notice the order the balance forces on you. You can't share the pans into equal groups while loose unit tiles sit next to the x-tiles — so the units must be cleared FIRST, and the splitting comes LAST. That is exactly why, on paper, you subtract before you divide.
A heavier equation — watch the equation line update with every move.

widget.prompt: Solve 3x + 6 = 18. Keep one eye on the equation above the beam as you work.
widget.successFeedback: x = 4. The equation line walked with you: 3x + 6 = 18 → 3x = 12 → x = 4. The tiles and the algebra are the same moves.
widget.unbalancedFeedback: Tipped — a removal wasn't paired. The equation line shows a left side and right side that are no longer equal at the same x. Undo and re-pair.
widget.notIsolatedFeedback: Level, but unfinished. Six units have to leave BOTH pans before the three-way split becomes fair.
widget.missFeedback: Keep all three x-tiles. Clear the six unit tiles from each side, then split both sides into 3 equal groups.

explanationVariants: Clear 2 units from each pan (5x = 15), then split both sides into 5 groups: x = 3.
Two fair moves: an equal removal, then an equal share-out. The beam stays level through both, which is the proof each move was legal.

widget.prompt: On the balance, remove the loose 2s first, then split the remaining tiles for 5x + 2 = 17.
widget.successFeedback: x = 3. Two units off each side, then a five-way split — and the beam never moved.
widget.unbalancedFeedback: The tip means the sides no longer weigh the same. Every removal needs its twin on the other pan. Undo to level and pair up.
widget.notIsolatedFeedback: Balanced but not done — x still shares its pan. Finish clearing units from both sides, then split.
widget.missFeedback: Leave the x-tiles alone; they're the unknown you're isolating. Units off both sides first, then split both sides into 5 groups.

steps.body: Now without tiles. Solve it on paper the way the balance made you solve it with your hands.
explanationVariants: Subtract 7 from both sides: 4x = 24. Divide both sides by 4: x = 6.
The balance order, in symbols: the + 7 is cleared first (it's loose units), and the ×4 is undone last (it's the share-out).

commonErrors.feedback: That's 4x, not x — the units are cleared (31 − 7 = 24) but the four-way split hasn't happened. Divide both sides by 4: x = 6.
That divided before subtracting — sharing out the pans while 7 loose units still sat on the left. Clear the + 7 first: (31 − 7) ÷ 4 = 6.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Balance order: subtract 7 from both sides (4x = 24), then divide both sides by 4 (x = 6).

explanationVariants: Four units off each pan leaves 6x = 24; a six-way split of both sides gives x = 4.
Two-step equations are always these same two fair moves: equal removal, then equal share-out — the size of the numbers changes nothing.
hints: Which tiles are stopping you from splitting right now — the x-tiles or the loose units?
Clear the 4 loose units, one from each pan at a time, until the left pan is pure x-tiles.
With 6x = 24 on the pans, split both sides into 6 equal groups: each x-tile matches 4 units.

widget.prompt: Solve 6x + 4 = 28 on the balance, checking after each move that both pans remain equal.
widget.successFeedback: x = 4, and the beam never tipped. Equal removal, equal share-out — that pair of moves solves every equation in this chapter.
widget.unbalancedFeedback: Tipped. Somewhere a tile left one pan alone. Undo until the beam is level again, then remove strictly in pairs.
widget.notIsolatedFeedback: Level so far — every move fair. Keep going: all four loose units off both sides, then the six-way split.
widget.missFeedback: Six x-tiles stay put — they're the unknown. Take the four unit tiles off each pan, then split both sides into 6 groups.

takeaways: An equation is a level beam: any move that touches only one side breaks the equality — and the beam shows it instantly.
The balance forces the solving order: clear loose units from both sides FIRST, split into equal groups LAST — which is why on paper you subtract before you divide.
steps.teaser: Next: equations where the x-tiles come wrapped in parentheses — and the balance needs one extra move before it can help.
steps.body: Two fair moves solved every equation today — and the beam was the referee.
